strengths: Clear motivation and paradigm shift: The paper convincingly identifies the key bottlenecks of centralized routers—namely parameter-constrained inaccuracy and inflexibility to pool modifications—and offers a well-formulated distributed alternative based on LLM self-awareness.

Well-designed training pipeline: The two-stage training strategy (SFT with selective rejection and RL with a scenario-conditioned reward) elegantly decentralizes the training process, enabling each agent to optimize its local policy independently and adapt to various performance-cost preferences (alpha) via prompt conditioning.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Experiments cover a wide range of benchmarks (7 in-domain and 3 out-of-domain datasets) and compare against strong existing routing baselines (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT, Automix, FORC, GraphRouter), showing consistent utility gains.

Rigorous supporting analyses: The authors provide thoughtful analyses verifying that performance gains stem from improved self-awareness rather than task-knowledge leakage (Appendix J), demonstrating plug-and-play modularity when removing models from the pool (Table 4), and evaluating the marginal token overhead of rejection (Appendix A).
weaknesses: Reliance on model fine-tuning limits applicability to open-weights models: DiSRouter requires full supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on each model in the pool. This fundamentally restricts the framework to open-weights models and prevents the inclusion of proprietary, black-box frontier LLM APIs (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet), which are common in real-world LLM routing systems.

Cascading latency and infrastructure overhead: Although generating a short rejection sequence ('I don't know!') uses few decoding steps, sequential routing across models (e.g., 0.5B -> 1.5B -> 3B -> 7B -> 14B) still incurs cumulative prompt prefill latency and round-trip communication overhead. Moreover, serving a live cascade requires hosting multiple models concurrently in memory.

Narrow empirical instantiation compared to conceptual claims: While Section 1 and Section 6 discuss general distributed topologies (e.g., trees or meshes), the actual implementation and experiments are strictly limited to a linear cascade among homogeneous models from a single family (Qwen2.5).

strengths: Clear conceptual motivation: shifting query routing from a monolithic centralized router to distributed, agent-level self-awareness addresses key rigidity issues when adding or removing models.

Well-structured training pipeline: the two-stage alignment approach (SFT for abstention formatting followed by RL with a scenario-conditioned reward) provides an intuitive and effective way to calibrate LLM confidence across different cost-performance tradeoffs.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper tests across 10 diverse benchmarks (both in-domain and out-of-domain), three preference scenarios, and compares against an extensive set of routing baselines (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT, AutoMix, FORC, GraphRouter).

Insightful diagnostic experiments: the authors include helpful sanity checks, such as verifying that task-solving capability itself was not substantially altered by fine-tuning (Appendix J) and showing that internal self-assessment out-predicts external classifiers.
weaknesses: Incompatibility with proprietary/black-box models: DiSRouter requires full SFT and RL alignment for every model in the pool. In many realistic routing scenarios, high-end models are closed-source commercial APIs (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) where parameter updates are impossible.

Latency and cumulative overhead in cascading: When a query is hard and reaches the 14B model, it sequentially traverses four intermediate models (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B). Although generating 'I don't know' takes few decoding tokens, each hop incurs full prompt prefill, context processing, and sequential network latency, which degrades user-perceived turnaround time compared to direct 1-hop routing.

Evaluation restricted to homogeneous linear cascades: While the paper mentions general network topologies (such as trees or meshes), the actual formulation and experiments are limited strictly to a linear cascade over the homogeneous Qwen2.5 family, leaving open questions about how the method handles heterogeneous models with non-monotonic capability profiles.

Simplified cost accounting: Equation (1) and the evaluation assign cost solely based on the final executing model, ignoring the cumulative GPU FLOPs and prefill compute consumed by all preceding rejecting models in the cascade.

strengths: Innovative perspective shifting query routing from centralized external controllers to distributed, intrinsic self-awareness and self-routing across LLMs.
Well-formulated two-stage training pipeline (Self-Awareness SFT and scenario-conditioned RL) that incorporates user preferences directly into the models' abstention behaviors.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation comparing against a wide array of representative routing baselines (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT, Automix, FORC, GraphRouter) across 7 in-domain and 3 out-of-domain datasets.

Insightful diagnostic analyses, particularly Table 5 showing intrinsic self-assessment outperforming external classifiers and Appendix J demonstrating that routing gains do not merely stem from improved task reasoning.
weaknesses: Unrealistic cost and latency assumptions: The formulation defines total query cost as only the inference cost of the final executing model, ignoring the prompt prefill and generation overhead incurred by upstream models along the cascade trajectory. In practice, sequential hops accumulate significant latency and token-processing costs.

High barrier to deployment and incompatibility with closed-source models: The framework requires full SFT and RL fine-tuning for every model in the pool. This severely restricts its practical utility in real-world routing scenarios that involve proprietary or black-box APIs (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude) which cannot be fine-tuned.

Gap between conceptual framing and actual implementation: While the paper motivates the framework around complex distributed network structures (trees, meshes), the actual implementation and evaluation are confined strictly to a standard linear cascade with learned refusal behavior.

Marginal utility gains in challenging settings: On out-of-domain benchmarks under the cost-first setting (Table 14), DiSRouter yields only modest improvements over existing baselines such as FrugalGPT.

strengths: Well-motivated paradigm shift: Moving from centralized external scoring routers to a decentralized self-routing framework effectively tackles the inflexibility and knowledge boundary blindness inherent to small external routers.

Sound and independent training pipeline: The two-stage Self-Awareness Training (SFT + RL) with a scenario-conditioned reward (1 - alpha)^gamma allows each model to be trained fully in parallel and locally, adjusting its rejection threshold dynamically according to user preferences.

Strong empirical performance: DiSRouter consistently outperforms competitive centralized routing baselines (such as GraphRouter, RouteLLM, FORC, and FrugalGPT) across various cost-accuracy trade-off scenarios on seven standard benchmarks.

Extensive analysis and robustness checks: The appendix provides thorough investigations, including modularity tests (reducing agent pools without retraining), latency/overhead measurements, validation across heterogeneous model families (Gemma-3, Phi-4), and intrinsic self-awareness evaluations on proprietary models.
weaknesses: Cascade limitation in empirical evaluation: While the conceptual framework discusses general distributed topologies (e.g., trees or meshes), the actual implementation and experiments are strictly restricted to a sequential linear cascade ordered by model size.

Cost formulation omits intermediate invocations: Equation (1) and Section 2.1 define the total cost as solely the cost of the final executing model, ignoring the cumulative prompt-processing and token-generation costs incurred by earlier rejecting models along the cascade path.

Model modification overhead: Unlike external routers that treat candidate LLMs as black-box models, DiSRouter requires fine-tuning (both SFT and RL) for each open-source model in the pool, which can become compute-intensive to deploy and maintain across large model ecosystems.

strengths: Conceptual shift and formulation: Shifting from centralized routing to distributed, agent-level self-awareness is conceptually elegant and addresses two core pain points of centralized routers—inflexibility when modifying the model pool and the inability of small external routers to accurately assess the knowledge boundaries of larger models.

Decoupled training design: The two-stage Self-Awareness Training pipeline (SFT + RL) with a localized, scenario-conditioned reward allows each agent to be trained completely independently and in parallel, while maintaining coordinated behavior via user preference prompts.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The authors evaluate across 10 diverse benchmarks (both in-domain and out-of-domain), compare against strong competitive router baselines (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT, AutoMix, FORC, GraphRouter), and consistently achieve superior utility across different preference regimes (Performance First, Balanced, Cost First).

Thorough analytical experiments: The paper includes extensive analysis answering key questions: modularity (removing models without retraining), external vs. intrinsic assessment accuracy, latency/time-overhead profiling, verification that underlying task capability is preserved (Pass@10 analysis), extension to heterogeneous model families (Gemma, Phi), and extension to continuous/open-ended generation tasks.
weaknesses: Cascade architecture scope: While the paper motivates a general distributed routing framework with prospective mesh or tree structures, the actual realization is restricted to a linear cascade ordered by model size. LLM cascades with abstention/delegation are an established design pattern, making the topological novelty somewhat more limited than implied by the general formulation.

Training requirement on constituent agents: Unlike black-box external routers that can route to off-the-shelf or proprietary models without altering them, DiSRouter requires full SFT and RL alignment on each constituent model in the pool (except for closed-source models evaluated via prompt engineering in the appendix).

Cumulative prefill and latency overhead: While rejection responses are short (few tokens), sequential cascades still incur latency and cumulative prefill compute across intermediate rejected stages before reaching the final executor. Although analyzed in Appendix A.1, this sequential overhead can become noticeable as cascade depth grows.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and timely problem in LLM serving: how to route queries cost-effectively among models of varying capabilities without relying on rigid, centralized external routers.

The proposed Self-Awareness Training pipeline (SFT followed by scenario-conditioned RL) is conceptually clean, well-grounded in utility theory, and enables models to adaptively shift their decision boundaries across performance-first and cost-first regimes using prompt conditioning.

Decoupling the routing mechanism into independent, localized agent decisions provides genuine modularity ('plug-and-play' capability), which is empirically validated by dropping or swapping models (e.g., adding Gemma-3 and Phi-4) without retraining the rest of the system.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, diverse model families, and comparison with strong routing baselines (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT, Automix, FORC, GraphRouter).

Thorough auxiliary analyses in the appendix, including latency analysis, confirmation that underlying task accuracy is not artificially inflated by the training (Pass@10 check), and preliminary extension to open-ended generation tasks.
weaknesses: The term 'distributed routing' is conceptually somewhat overclaimed given the actual implementation. In practice, the system operates as a sequential cascade / waterfall architecture (ordered from smallest to largest LLM). While non-linear topologies (trees/meshes) are discussed, they are not empirically demonstrated.

The sequential nature of the cascade introduces cumulative latency and serving overhead for hard queries that must sequentially fail on multiple small models before being handled by the largest model. Although the rejection output is short, network round-trips and queueing times in distributed production environments could be non-trivial.

Unlike external routers where only a single small classifier is trained, DiSRouter requires fine-tuning and running RL on every candidate LLM in the pool (except the largest fallback model), which incurs non-trivial upfront alignment cost.

The extension to open-ended generation tasks (Appendix A.11) relies on percentile-based score distributions from a predefined metric/reward model, which reintroduces dependency on external scoring models for non-verifiable outputs.
